items.title: Arithmetic and precedence
items.meaning: Arithmetic operators calculate values: + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies. Multiplication is evaluated before addition unless parentheses change the grouping.
items.purpose: Use arithmetic for prices, scores, and damage. Work through the calculation in precedence order, rather than assuming every operation happens from left to right.

items.title: Comparisons and equality
items.meaning: A comparison produces true or false. == tests equality, while <, >, <=, and >= compare ordering. A single = assigns a value rather than comparing it.

items.title: Boolean logic
items.meaning: A boolean represents a true/false condition. Logical AND requires both conditions to succeed. One failed requirement makes an AND expression false.

items.title: Functions and return values

items.title: Parentheses and expression evaluation
items.meaning: Parentheses group an expression so that its value is calculated before the surrounding operations use it. This can change the result.
items.purpose: Use parentheses to make a rule explicit when operators are mixed. Grouping is also useful when it improves readability without changing the result.
items.walkthrough: The grouped addition produces nine before multiplication produces 27.

items.title: Stacks and last-in-first-out
items.meaning: A stack removes the most recently added element first. This is last-in-first-out, or LIFO. A pop both returns and removes the top element.
items.purpose: Use stacks for undo history or backtracking. Check that a stack contains an item before popping; removing from an empty stack is an error.
items.walkthrough: tower was added after gate, so it is the first value removed.

items.title: Integer division inside a loop
items.meaning: An accumulator can combine the results of another operation. For positive values, integer division keeps the complete groups and discards any fractional part.
items.purpose: Use this pattern when leftovers from separate batches cannot be pooled. Dividing each batch before summing is different from summing all batches before division. Integer division truncates toward zero; these inputs are all positive.

items.title: Base cases and recursive progress
items.meaning: A base case returns without another recursive call. The recursive step must make progress toward that case; merely having a base case does not guarantee termination.
items.purpose: Choose a stopping condition that covers the values a recursive step can reach. Subtracting by more than one can pass below zero, so equality with zero may be insufficient.

items.title: Variables and data types
items.meaning: A variable is a named place to keep a value. Later statements can read it or replace it. A type describes the kinds of values and operations that are permitted.
items.purpose: Use clear names for changing state such as ammunition or health. Read the right side of an assignment before replacing the value on its left. Python determines the type from the assigned value.
items.code_snippet:
arrows = 18
arrows = arrows + 4
print(arrows)
items.walkthrough: The variable starts at 18, then adds four and stores 22. The output reads the updated value.

items.title: Arithmetic and precedence
items.meaning: Arithmetic operators calculate values: + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies. Multiplication is evaluated before addition unless parentheses change the grouping.
items.purpose: Use arithmetic for prices, scores, and damage. Work through the calculation in precedence order, rather than assuming every operation happens from left to right.
items.code_snippet:
pouches = 5
coins = pouches * 7 + 4
print(coins)
items.walkthrough: Multiplication produces 35 before addition contributes four more.

items.title: Output and joining strings
items.meaning: A string is a sequence of text characters. Joining two strings with + produces a new string; it does not insert spaces automatically.
items.purpose: Use output for messages and debugging. Put spaces and punctuation inside the text literals, and pay attention to the difference between text and numbers.
items.code_snippet:
hero = "Mira"
print("Welcome, " + hero)
items.walkthrough: The greeting literal supplies its trailing space. Joining the name produces one message.

items.title: Comparisons and equality
items.meaning: A comparison produces true or false. == tests equality, while <, >, <=, and >= compare ordering. A single = assigns a value rather than comparing it.
items.purpose: Use comparisons to decide whether a requirement is met. Check whether your rule includes the boundary value: >= includes equality, but > does not.
items.code_snippet:
rank = 7
print(rank == 7)
items.walkthrough: Both sides are seven, so equality succeeds.
items.prompt: What does the practice example print? Trace it before revealing the answer.

items.title: Boolean logic
items.meaning: A boolean represents a true/false condition. Logical AND requires both conditions to succeed. One failed requirement makes an AND expression false.
items.purpose: Use combined conditions for gates or abilities with more than one requirement. Name the separate conditions when doing so makes a rule easier to read. The logical AND operator is and.
items.code_snippet:
hasMap = True
energy = 9
print(hasMap and energy > 5)
items.walkthrough: Both the map condition and the energy comparison succeed.
items.prompt: What does the practice example print? Trace it before revealing the answer.

items.title: Indexes in arrays and lists
items.meaning: An index identifies a position in an ordered collection. Nonnegative indexes start at zero, so index 1 is the second element.
items.purpose: Use indexing to retrieve one particular item. For a nonempty collection of size n, its final ordinary nonnegative index is n - 1.
items.code_snippet:
supplies = [6, 13, 21]
print(supplies[1])
items.walkthrough: Index 1 selects the second position, which contains 13.

items.title: Functions and return values
items.meaning: A function groups reusable instructions. Parameters receive inputs. return sends a result back to the caller; printing a value instead only displays it.
items.purpose: Use functions to avoid repeating calculations. The caller can store, print, or combine a returned result. A function should make its expected inputs and result clear. Python declares a function with def.
items.walkthrough: The parameters receive 7 and 5. The function returns their sum, then the caller prints it.

items.title: Counting loops
items.meaning: A counting loop repeats a block while a counter advances through a range. Initialization chooses the first value, and the condition decides whether another iteration runs.
items.purpose: Use counting loops for a known number of repetitions. Check the upper boundary carefully so the loop runs neither one too many times nor one too few. Python range excludes its stop argument.
items.code_snippet:
for step in range(2, 5):
    print(step)
items.walkthrough: The counter visits 2, 3, and 4. It stops before 5.
items.prompt: What does the practice example print? Trace it before revealing the answer.

items.explanation: The range starts at 4 and excludes 7, so three values are printed.

items.title: Assignment and statement syntax
items.meaning: Assignment replaces the value stored in a variable. The expression on the right can read the old value before the new one is stored.
items.purpose: Use assignment to update state. Statement endings and block structure are part of the language syntax; missing or misplaced syntax can prevent code from running. Python uses newlines for these statements and indentation for blocks.
items.code_snippet:

shield = shield - 5
print(shield)
items.walkthrough: The old value is used to calculate 14 - 5 before shield is replaced.

items.title: If and else branches
items.meaning: An if statement chooses a block using a boolean condition. An optional else block runs when the condition is false.
items.purpose: Use branches for actions that depend on current state. In a single if/else pair only one branch runs, so trace the condition before reading its output.

items.title: Accumulating a total
items.meaning: An accumulator is updated repeatedly to combine a sequence of values. A sum normally starts at zero, the value that changes nothing when added.
items.purpose: Use this pattern for total coins, damage, or measurements. Initialize the accumulator outside the loop so each iteration keeps the earlier work.
items.code_snippet:
total = 0
for wave in range(1, 5):
    total = total + wave
print(total)

items.title: Selecting part of a string
items.meaning: A substring or slice selects a section of text by position. The exact meaning of the second argument depends on the language.
items.purpose: Use substring operations for prefixes and fragments. Distinguish an end index from a character count; Java, C#, and Python do not all use the same convention. Python [start:stop] excludes stop.

items.title: Safe collection iteration
items.meaning: The size of a collection counts its elements. Because indexing begins at zero, an index equal to the size is already past the end.
items.purpose: Use the actual collection size rather than a hard-coded loop endpoint. This keeps the loop correct when the collection grows or shrinks.

items.title: Compound assignment
items.meaning: A compound assignment combines an operation with storing its result. For these integers, x += amount adds amount to x and replaces x with that result.
items.purpose: Use compound assignment for counters and running totals when it improves readability. It changes a value; it is not an equality comparison.
items.code_snippet:
charge = 12
charge += 3
charge *= 2
print(charge)

items.title: Comparing string contents
items.meaning: Value equality asks whether text contains the same characters. Object identity asks whether two references identify the same object; that is a different question.
items.purpose: Use a value comparison for commands and labels. Ordinary comparisons in these examples are case-sensitive, so capitalization matters. Python == compares values; is tests identity.
items.code_snippet:

print(password == "rune")

items.title: Collection size and final index
items.meaning: Size counts positions, not distinct values. Repeated elements still occupy separate positions. For a nonempty collection the final index is size - 1.
items.purpose: Use size to display item counts or control iteration. Do not subtract one when you want a count; subtract one only when you need a final valid index.

items.title: Parameters and reusable calculations
items.meaning: Parameters are local names for the values supplied at a call site. Changing the arguments can change a function result without changing its instructions.
items.purpose: Separate an algorithm from its input data. Check argument order: swapping two inputs can change which one gets multiplied or otherwise transformed.

items.title: The remainder operator
items.meaning: For positive integers, a % b is what remains after making complete groups of size b. It differs from the quotient produced by division.
items.purpose: Use remainders for cycles and even/odd checks. These examples use positive integers; negative-operand remainder rules differ between languages.
items.code_snippet:

print(crystals % 6)
items.walkthrough: Three groups of six use eighteen crystals. Five remain.

items.title: Skipping iterations with continue
items.meaning: continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration. It does not finish the whole loop; later iterations can still run.
items.purpose: Use continue to ignore an unwanted item and process the remaining items. Use break when you intend to stop the loop altogether.

items.title: Updating an indexed element
items.meaning: An indexed assignment replaces a single element. Reading from one index and writing to another does not move every element in the collection.
items.purpose: Use indexed updates for inventory slots or saved scores. Check both indexes before tracing the expression: the source and destination positions can be different.

items.title: Recursion and returned results
items.meaning: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Its returned results are combined as the earlier calls finish.
items.purpose: Use recursion for naturally repeating subproblems. Trace both the calls going toward the base case and the results returning toward the original caller. This function expects a nonnegative integer input.

items.title: Binary search on sorted data
items.meaning: Binary search compares a target with the middle element of sorted data, then discards the half that cannot contain the target.
items.purpose: Use it for lookups in sorted data. Each step approximately halves the search interval, giving O(log n) search time. Sorting itself has a separate cost.

items.title: Growing collections
items.meaning: A dynamic collection can grow when elements are added. Appending an element adds a new position rather than replacing an existing one.
items.purpose: Use a dynamic collection when the item count can change. Its current size describes how many elements it contains, not how much capacity may be reserved internally. Use append and len for Python lists.
items.code_snippet:
bag = ["map", "torch"]
bag.append("rope")
print(len(bag))
items.walkthrough: The worked bag ends with map, torch, and rope: three entries.

items.title: Object identity and value equality
items.meaning: Separately created objects have different identities even if their fields match. A custom class can define what equality of its values should mean.
items.purpose: Define value equality explicitly for domain objects. This example compares a rune power field. In hash-based collections, equality and hashing must obey a consistent contract. Python uses __eq__ for ==. Defining __eq__ alone does not make this class hashable; __hash__ is a separate contract.

items.title: Exceptions and recovery
items.meaning: An exception signals that an operation could not finish normally. A matching catch or except handler can choose how to recover from that failure.
items.purpose: Handle failures you can meaningfully recover from. Catch the specific error you expect instead of silently swallowing every possible problem.

items.title: List comprehensions
items.meaning: A list comprehension builds a new list by transforming items from an iterable, optionally including only items that pass a condition.
items.purpose: Use a typed collection to catch invalid element usage early, or use a short comprehension to express a clear transformation. Keep transformations readable. A Python comprehension writes the output expression before for and an optional filter after if.
items.code_snippet:
values = [1, 2, 3]
boosted = [n * 3 for n in values if n > 1]
print(boosted)
items.walkthrough: The condition excludes one. The remaining inputs, two and three, are multiplied by three.
